item.title: Why Someone Next to You Gets Better Cell Service at Crowded Events
item.content:encoded: The article explains how LTE's Quality of Service Class Identifier (QCI) and its 5G equivalent, 5QI, determine which users receive network priority during congestion. It compares how Verizon, AT&T, T-Mobile, and major MVNOs assign priority levels, clarifies common misconceptions about "premium data," and helps readers choose a plan based on real-world network performance rather than marketing claims.

item.title: Making Toponymy Accessible Through Maps, AI, and Interactive Learning
item.content:encoded: The article argues that toponymy, the study of place names, is largely absent from modern education despite its cultural and historical value. It introduces Name of the World, an interactive EdTech platform that combines maps, quizzes, AI-assisted explanations, and verified geographic data to make learning the origins of place names more engaging. A pilot involving 347 students showed significant improvements in knowledge retention and positive feedback on the interactive learning approach.

item.title: Stablecoins vs. Banks: Who'll Rewire Finance First?
item.content:encoded: Stablecoins have evolved from niche crypto tools into a core component of global finance, driven by new regulatory frameworks in the U.S. and Hong Kong. Rather than replacing banks, stablecoins are increasingly being adopted by them, creating a hybrid financial model that combines the trust and compliance of traditional institutions with the speed and programmability of blockchain networks. The future of finance is unlikely to be a battle between banks and crypto; instead, it will be defined by how effectively the two are integrated.

item.title: Robotics - The Wave After AI

item.title: Static Analysis of Linux Malware Captured by a Cowrie Honeypot
item.content:encoded: When a bot thinks it has logged into a small energy device, it installs commodity Linux malware. This is a static, defensive breakdown of what a honeypot captured after weak SSH and Telnet logins: fake-daemon binaries that masquerade as sshd and xinetd, a statically linked bot, a backdoor with three independent persistence mechanisms, and a self-deleting campaign visible only through commands. The payloads are ordinary, but the chain is the lesson: weak login, host fingerprint, payload staging, persistence, and reach-out. Default-deny egress breaks the last step.

item.title: What Most AI Startup Founders Get Wrong About AI Agents "The Autonomy Trap"
item.content:encoded:
Most AI startup founders are chasing autonomy too early and that’s a mistake.
AI agents today are not reliable enough to replace full workflows. Systems that look impressive in demos often break in real-world conditions due to reasoning gaps, context loss, and edge cases.
The startups that succeed take a different approach: They don’t try to automate everything. They focus on high-value, narrow workflows, keep humans in the loop, and expand autonomy gradually.
The real competitive advantage is no longer the AI model it’s the system around it: reliability, observability, workflow integration, and trust.
The future isn’t fully autonomous AI. It’s supervised intelligence at scale.

Core principle: anything you state in code costs tokens; anything the compiler infers is free.

item.title: I Built a PC Monitor That Learns Your Hardware
item.content:encoded:
Every traditional PC monitor — Afterburner, HWiNFO, CCleaner, GeForce Experience — runs on absolute thresholds and general profiles. "If temp over 80, alert." But your machine isn't in any table: silicon lottery, component aging, ambient temperature, and load composition mean a generic profile describes a computer you don't own. The fix is statistics on YOUR history, not the manufacturer's spec — median + MAD with Nelson Rules (the same Statistical Process Control factories use), workload-bucketed thermal baselines via Welford's algorithm, all running locally and offline with zero telemetry. A PSU rail sagging to 11.7V is "in spec" to a threshold but a 5-sigma anomaly against your own learned 11.95-12.05V norm — caught months before failure. Not a chatbot bolted on. Real statistics that don't hallucinate. It's working open-source code in PC Workman v1.7.9, built solo over 11 months between physical-labor shifts.

item.title: Your AI Chat Will Break in Production: 3 Lifecycle Bugs Nobody Warns You About
item.content:encoded:

Three fixes: (1) Stream Identity — unique ID per stream, every callback checks if it's still current; (2) Explicit Cleanup — close the connection, mark the chat stale, force-fetch on return; (3) Resume, not restart — pick the stream up from a sequence cursor instead of regenerating. Underlying rule: push-based data shouldn't live in React state directly.
